sentences.text: Dyrosaurus is an extinct genus of crocodylomorph that lived during the Early Eocene.
The name combines the Greek word for lizard or reptile with the mountain Djebel Dyr near the discovery site of the type species.
The type species possessed thin jaws with numerous recurved teeth, indicating a predominantly fish-eating diet similar to the modern Gharial.
French paleontologist Auguste Pomel named the genus in 1894 after Djebel Dyr mountain in Algeria, where fossilized vertebrae were found in a phosphate mine.
The first remains were originally named Crocodilus phosphaticus by Thomas in 1893 based on Early Eocene fossils from Gafsa, Tunisia.
Giuseppe de Stefano named the family Dyrosauridae in 1903, referencing the holotype locality in Djebel Dyr, Algeria.
Thévenin recognized in 1911 that Dyrosaurus phosphaticus was a Lower Eocene crocodyliform based on better preserved material.
Dyrosaurus teeth had a smooth enamel layer and were long and frequently sharp, helping it hunt fast-moving prey.
It is likely that Dyrosaurus shared a lifestyle similar to modern crocodylomorphs.
Dyrosaurus belongs to the family Dyrosauridae.
Dyrosaurus is classified within the superorder Crocodylomorpha.
Dyrosaurus is part of the unranked family Neosuchia.
D. phosphaticus fossils have been found in Algeria and Tunisia, while D. maghribensis fossils have only been found in Morocco.
The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Dyrosaurus as Albian to Priabonian (113.2 to 33.9 million years ago).
